sections.what_happened: [ANALYSIS / MARKET DATA] UBS raised its Brent forecast for the second time in October to $110/barrel at end-2026 (from $100; 2027 curve lifted $5 at each point to $95 Mar, $90 Jun, $85 Sep), per OilPrice reporting of the UBS note. UBS: Middle Eastern crude loadings recovered substantially from severe disruption earlier in 2026 but Gulf crude/condensate port loadings remain below prewar levels; October brought a record number of reported attacks on vessels in/around Hormuz, raising insurance and freight costs; very large crude carrier (VLCC) rates Middle East-China climbed to $30-40/barrel against $1-3 over the past decade; pledged strategic-reserve releases are largely complete. Spot check Wed: Brent ~$115.30-115.69, WTI ~$101.90-102.42 (Reuters via Dawn/NDTV Profit/DTN). This is a forecast + freight-cost figure, not a counted transit figure; PortWatch Hormuz counts remain STALE (obs. 2026-10-18: 4 transits, 7-day avg 3.7 vs 2025 baseline 85.5/day) and are cited only as stale.
sections.what_verified: OilPrice (T3) for the UBS note; spot prices Reuters (T1) via Dawn/NDTV Profit.
sections.why_matters: Pocketbook lane: the war tax on every barrel -- $30-40 freight where $1-3 was normal, and a bank now pricing $110 into year-end.
sections.context: Background: MARKET DATA (Wed Oct 28) -- UBS raises Brent year-end forecast to $110; VLCC Middle East-China rates $30-40/barrel vs $1-3 over past decade; Gulf loadings still below prewar

totw_analysis: Our read: Pocketbook lane: the war tax on every barrel -- $30-40 freight where $1-3 was normal, and a bank now pricing $110 into year-end. The fault line our audience is arguing over: Who pays for the shipping war -- producers, shippers, or households at the pump?
